title: FIR Filters, FFT Convolution and Wavelets
description: Ten original questions on filter ideals, window design, linear phase, FFT convolution, STFT resolution, Haar DWT and translation invariance. Multiple-response scoring is for practice only: +1 per correct selection and -0.5 per incorrect selection, floored at zero.

questions.prompt: Which statements distinguish ideal low-pass and high-pass filters?

options.content: An ideal low-pass filter passes frequencies near DC.
An ideal high-pass filter suppresses frequencies near DC.
Both are described by passband and stopband regions separated by a cutoff in the ideal model.
They have identical magnitude responses at every frequency.

questions.explanation: Low-pass and high-pass filters select complementary low- and high-frequency regions. Their ideal responses change abruptly at a cutoff, though practical designs require a transition band.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 3, ideal filter review

questions.prompt: Why can an ideal brick-wall frequency response not be implemented exactly as a finite, causal FIR filter?

options.content: Its inverse transform has an impulse response extending infinitely in time.
A zero-phase ideal response produces a two-sided impulse response.
A practical FIR design must truncate or window an ideal response.
A finite number of taps can reproduce an arbitrary discontinuous ideal response exactly.

questions.explanation: An abrupt frequency discontinuity corresponds to an infinite-duration sinc-like impulse response. Causal FIR design therefore delays and truncates or windows it, introducing transition width and ripple.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 3 Tutorial, ideal filter and window-design questions

questions.prompt: In the window method for FIR design, which trade-offs are generally relevant?

options.content: A longer window can produce a narrower transition band.
Window choice affects sidelobe level and passband or stopband ripple.
Abrupt rectangular truncation tends to produce stronger sidelobes than smoother windows.
Window length and shape have no effect on the realized frequency response.

questions.explanation: Longer filters improve frequency resolution, while smoother windows reduce sidelobes at the cost of a broader mainlobe. The window therefore controls transition width and ripple together.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 3, common windows and filter design

questions.prompt: For a Kaiser-window FIR design, which qualitative roles are correct?

options.content: The Kaiser shape parameter controls the sidelobe-versus-mainlobe trade-off.
Filter length is strongly related to the required transition width.
Stricter attenuation or a narrower transition generally requires more taps.
One tap can meet any arbitrary magnitude specification if the shape parameter is large enough.

questions.explanation: Kaiser design offers a tunable window shape, but demanding attenuation and narrow transitions still require sufficient filter order. The shape parameter alone cannot replace the required number of taps.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 3 Tutorial, Kaiser-window Questions 2-3

questions.prompt: Which property of a real FIR impulse response is used to obtain generalized linear phase?

options.content: The coefficients are symmetric or antisymmetric about their midpoint.
The coefficients are independent random values.
Every coefficient is strictly positive.
The impulse response has infinite duration.

questions.explanation: Real FIR filters with midpoint symmetry or antisymmetry have generalized linear phase. The symmetry factors the response into a real amplitude term and a linear phase term.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 3, Type 1-4 FIR linear-phase systems

questions.prompt: Sequences have lengths $Lx$ and $Lh$. Which statements about FFT-based convolution are correct?

options.content: Their full linear convolution has length $Lx+Lh-1$.
Using a DFT length at least $Lx+Lh-1$ avoids time-domain aliasing.
After padding, multiply the DFTs and take the inverse DFT.
Without sufficient padding, circular convolution is always identical to full linear convolution.

questions.explanation: DFT multiplication produces circular convolution. Padding to at least the linear-convolution length prevents wraparound overlap, so the inverse DFT equals the desired linear result.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 3, fast convolution slides 39-55 and Tutorial Q4

questions.prompt: What distinctions between STFT and wavelet analysis are illustrated by the diagram?

image.alt: Side-by-side time-frequency grids: equal STFT cells and wavelet cells that become wider at lower frequency.

options.content: A fixed STFT window gives one time-frequency resolution across the plane.
Wavelets use multiple scales and therefore multiresolution analysis.
Coarser time resolution can be paired with finer frequency resolution at low frequencies.
Both methods provide arbitrarily fine time and frequency resolution simultaneously.

questions.explanation: A single STFT window fixes the cell shape. Wavelet scale changes provide short windows at high frequency and long windows at low frequency. Neither method escapes the fundamental time-frequency resolution trade-off.

questions.prompt: In one level of a Haar discrete wavelet transform, what do the two analysis branches represent?

options.content: A low-pass branch captures local averages or coarse content.
A high-pass branch captures local differences or detail.
Each filtered branch is downsampled in the critically sampled DWT.
Both branches contain identical coefficients for every input.

questions.explanation: The Haar low-pass filter forms averages and the high-pass filter forms differences. Downsampling retains the same total number of coefficients across the two branches for a critically sampled transform.

questions.prompt: A critically sampled DWT is generally not translation invariant because shifting the input can change which samples survive each downsampling step.

options.content: True
False

questions.explanation: Downsampling ties the coefficients to a sampling phase. Even a one-sample input shift can produce a very different coefficient pattern, motivating stationary or cycle-spun alternatives.

questions.prompt: Which steps belong to a spin-cycle wavelet procedure?

options.content: Circularly shift the input by several offsets.
Apply the wavelet-domain operation to each shifted version.
Invert each shift after reconstruction and average the results.
It always uses fewer coefficients and less computation than one ordinary DWT.

questions.explanation: Cycle spinning repeats the transform over multiple circular shifts, undoes the shifts and averages. This reduces shift sensitivity but creates an overcomplete and more computationally expensive procedure.
questions.source: EE3731C Classical Signal 4, slides 41-44 and Tutorial 4 Question 1
